questions.q: In `class EchoClient(APIClient):`, what does `EchoClient` automatically get from `APIClient`?
options: Nothing — every method must be redefined in the subclass
Only the attributes, never the methods
Every attribute and method `APIClient` defines, unless `EchoClient` overrides one
Only methods whose names start with an underscore
questions.explain: A subclass inherits everything from its parent class automatically. It only needs to redefine (override) the specific methods it wants to behave differently.

questions.q: If both `Animal` and its subclass `Dog` define a method called `speak()`, which one runs when you call `Dog().speak()`?
options: `Dog`'s version, because Python checks the instance's own class first
`Animal`'s version, because parent methods always take priority
Both run, one after another
It raises a naming-conflict error
questions.explain: This is overriding: when a subclass defines a method with the same name, its version is used instead of the parent's, unless the subclass explicitly calls the parent's via `super()`.

questions.q: What does `super().__init__(api_key)` do inside a subclass's `__init__`?
options: Deletes the parent class entirely
Calls the parent class's `__init__` method, reusing its setup logic
Creates a brand-new, unrelated object
Is only valid syntax in Python 2, not Python 3
questions.explain: super() gives you a reference to the parent class, so super().__init__(api_key) runs the parent's __init__ — commonly used so a subclass can extend setup logic instead of duplicating it.

questions.q: Given `class LoggingClient(APIClient):`, what does `isinstance(lc, APIClient)` return for an instance `lc` of `LoggingClient`?
options: It raises a TypeError, since `lc` isn't literally an `APIClient`
False, because `lc` is a `LoggingClient`, not an `APIClient`
`None`, since isinstance doesn't work across inheritance
True, because a `LoggingClient` is a kind of `APIClient` through inheritance
questions.explain: isinstance() respects the inheritance chain — any instance of a subclass also counts as an instance of each of its parent classes.

questions.q: Why do real AI SDKs commonly use a base exception class (e.g. `APIError`) with more specific exceptions (like `RateLimitError`) inheriting from it?
options: So catching the base class also catches every more specific error beneath it, letting code handle errors broadly or specifically as needed
Because Python requires every exception to inherit from exactly one other exception
To make the error messages shorter
So that only the most specific exception type can ever be raised
questions.explain: Thanks to inheritance, an `except APIError:` block also catches `RateLimitError` and any other subclass of it, which is why SDKs build exception hierarchies rather than one flat list of unrelated error classes.
